writing.exampleCaption: Without `Box`, this enum would need infinite size.
writing.explanation:
A recursive type has no fixed size, because each level would contain another whole level. `Box` has a known pointer size, so putting the recursive part behind one makes the type representable. `Box` also lets a function return a trait object whose concrete size is not known at the call site.

A recursive enum needs a known size at compile time. If `Tree::Node` directly contained two more `Tree` values, each of those nodes would contain more nodes with no finite size the compiler could lay out. `Box<Tree>` replaces each child with a pointer whose size is known. The actual child values live in separate heap allocations, and the boxes own them. Dropping the root recursively drops the owned children.

The sample's `sum` function borrows `&Tree`, matches on its variants, and reads through the boxes. It does not take ownership of the tree just to traverse it. Trace a root with two leaves and predict the sum before running the code. Then add one nested node and observe how the recursive call follows a box. This exercise shows the separation between the size of the enum variant and the depth of the runtime tree.

A box is also a way to own a value whose concrete type is hidden behind a trait object, `Box<dyn Trait>`. The box does not make every operation faster: following pointers and allocating each node can cost more than a compact flat representation. Use it when indirection expresses a real need, such as recursion or owned dynamic dispatch. For a simple fixed set of values, a `Vec<T>` or plain struct may be clearer. Choose the data shape first, then the pointer type that makes it representable.

The box is an owning pointer, so moving the box moves ownership of the child allocation without copying the entire tree. That makes recursive construction manageable while preserving deterministic cleanup.
writing.feedback: `Box<List>` makes the recursive field pointer-sized and the type finite.

writing.summary: `Box` moves a value to the heap behind a single owner.

recall.question: Why does `sum` take `&Tree` rather than `Tree`, and how can it call `sum(l)` when `l` is a `&Box<Tree>`?
recall.answer: Traversal only reads, so borrowing avoids consuming the tree. Matching on `&Tree` binds `l` and `r` as `&Box<Tree>`, and deref coercion turns `&Box<Tree>` into the `&Tree` that `sum` expects.

recall.question: When is giving every node its own `Box` a poor choice of representation?
recall.answer: When no recursion or owned dynamic dispatch requires it: allocating each node and following pointers can cost more than a compact flat layout. For a simple fixed set of values, a `Vec<T>` or plain struct is often clearer.
